title: Resilience After Setbacks
summary: Reframe failure, run a blameless post-mortem, prepare a plan B and bounce back with small steps.
objectives: Reframe a failure into information and a next step.
Run a simple post-mortem on a setback.
Build a plan B and a bounce-back routine.

explanation.heading: Setbacks are inevitable
explanation.body: Everyone who tries ambitious things fails sometimes: a rejected application, a failed exam, a bug that breaks production. **Resilience** is not avoiding setbacks or hiding feelings; it is recovering and continuing with learning. It can be trained like a muscle. This lesson gives you four tools: reframing, a post-mortem, a plan B and a bounce-back routine. If setbacks leave you hopeless for weeks, talk to a trusted person or a counsellor.

explanation.heading: Reframing failure
explanation.body: Failure feels personal, but it is usually specific and temporary. Use three checks. **Specific**: "I failed this interview" is not "I am a failure". **Temporary**: this result is not permanent. **Informative**: what does it tell me? Replace "Why me?" with "What can I learn, and what will I try next?" Do not suppress feelings: allow a day or two to feel disappointed, talk to a friend and then move to action. Compare "I failed the viva, so I am not cut out for this" with "I forgot the key definition under pressure; I will practise answers aloud."

explanation.heading: The post-mortem
explanation.body: A **post-mortem** studies what happened to learn, not to blame. Sit down within a few days and write four headings. **What happened?** (facts only). **What went well?** (so you keep it). **What went wrong and why?** (look at causes, not character; ask why five times). **What will I change?** (two or three specific actions with dates). Keep it blameless: focus on processes, preparation and decisions. For a failed placement test: facts: scored 40 per cent, ran out of time on section two; cause: no timed practice; change: three timed mock tests by Sunday.

explanation.heading: Plan B and bouncing back
explanation.body: A **plan B** is a prepared alternative that reduces the fear of failing. For each important goal, write what you will do if it does not work: other companies to apply to, another exam date, a related role. Having a plan B does not mean lack of commitment; it frees you to commit fully. To **bounce back**, restore the basics first: sleep, food, movement and talking to someone. Then take one small step within 48 hours, such as booking a mock test. Small actions rebuild momentum. Track progress over weeks, not hours. Also remember that most successful people have a long list of rejections and failures behind them; what separates them is that they kept trying with better preparation each time. Treat each setback as one data point on a longer line, and let your plan B give you the security to keep going.

examples.title: A blameless post-mortem
examples.body: After a failed demo, Zoya writes: Facts: the database was not seeded. Cause: no pre-demo checklist. Change: build a five-point checklist and run it one hour before every demo.
examples.takeaway: A post-mortem turns embarrassment into a system fix.

examples.title: Plan B in action
examples.body: Aditya applies to ten SAP trainee roles. His plan B includes two junior web-development roles and an ABAP certification course. When early replies are slow, he feels less pressure and keeps learning.
examples.takeaway: Alternatives reduce fear and keep you moving.

exercises.prompt: Which is a healthy reframe of a rejection?
options: This application was not a fit; I will improve my resume and apply again.
exercises.why: It is specific, temporary and points to action.

exercises.prompt: A blameless post-mortem focuses on processes and ____, not on blaming people. (one word)
exercises.why: The aim is to learn from causes, not assign guilt.

exercises.prompt: Write a mini post-mortem for a real setback of yours using four headings: what happened, what went well, what went wrong and why, what I will change (two actions with dates).
exercises.modelAnswer: What happened: I scored 52 per cent on the mock technical test and ran out of time. Went well: I answered the easy questions accurately. Went wrong: I had never practised under a timer and spent too long on one question. Change: do two timed 30-minute practice sets by Saturday and set a rule to skip any question after three minutes.
exercises.guidance: Strong answers are factual, look at process causes and end with dated actions. Avoid statements such as "I am just bad at tests".

exercises.prompt: You failed an important exam and feel low. What is the best plan for the next 48 hours?

options.feedback: Isolation can deepen a low mood.

options.text: Rest, talk to someone you trust, and then book one small step such as reviewing your paper.
options.feedback: It restores basics and starts small action.

options.text: Decide to quit your course tonight.
options.feedback: Big decisions in distress are risky.

exercises.why: Restore basics, seek support and take one small step.

task.title: Run a post-mortem and set a plan B
task.brief: Review one setback and write a plan B for a current goal.
steps: Write the four post-mortem headings for one setback.
Write a plan B for one current goal.
Share the plan B with one person.
task.evidencePrompt: Write your two actions and your plan B.

quiz.prompt: A plan B helps because it:
After a setback, take one small step within ____ hours. (one word)
quiz.why: A step within 48 hours rebuilds momentum.

bank.prompt: Which question helps most after failure?
options: What can I learn and try next?
bank.why: It leads to learning and action.

reflection: What is a setback you have not fully learned from, and what would a blameless post-mortem say about it?

revision.redo: Write a post-mortem for another past setback in ten minutes.
